system_description.narrative_title: Great-power friction, AI governance, and market volatility
system_description.narrative_summary: The global order is an open, tightly coupled system where domestic politics, great-power rivalry, and rapid technological change interact with energy markets and monetary policy to produce frequent shocks. Key dynamics include a US political realignment that reshapes oversight and foreign policy; an intensifying US–China tech and AI competition highlighted by corporate-security crises; persistent high-stakes regional wars (Ukraine, the Middle East) that keep energy and security markets on edge; and sticky inflation forcing central banks to tighten policy. These processes feed on one another — market moves respond to geopolitical signals, tech governance becomes a national-security tool, and climate/energy transitions add an additional layer of stress.
system_description.scope: Nation-states and their foreign-policy choices, transnational security conflicts (Ukraine, Middle East), major technology firms and semiconductor/AI supply chains, global commodity and financial markets, and multilateral institutions and summits (e.g., COP31, IMF, G7).
system_description.super_system: The international system of states, markets, and transnational institutions that governs global security, economic stability, technology governance, and environmental stewardship.

variables.name: Russia-Ukraine war
variables.description: An ongoing high-intensity conflict between Russia and Ukraine marked by shifting frontlines, repeated strikes on infrastructure and intermittent diplomacy that together reshape European security dynamics.

variables.name: US–China tech and trade rivalry
variables.description: Strategic competition between the United States and China over semiconductors, AI and industrial policy, featuring export controls, corporate espionage concerns and partial decoupling of critical technology supply chains.

variables.name: Iran–Gulf regional confrontation
variables.description: A widening Iran-linked confrontation in the Gulf — including Houthi and proxy strikes on energy and infrastructure and heightened Gulf–US security cooperation — that risks chronic instability and disruptions to oil flows.

variables.name: Global inflation and monetary tightening
variables.description: Broad-based inflationary pressures across major economies are driving a synchronized and more aggressive cycle of central-bank rate hikes and rising sovereign yields, altering capital flows and market volatility worldwide.

variables.name: US political realignment and governance shifts
variables.description: Post-election changes in US domestic politics — congressional power shifts, new leadership and more aggressive oversight — are altering the policy trajectory on trade, technology regulation, foreign interventions and executive appointments.
